name: John Stuart Mill
role: British philosopher, economist and Liberal MP (1806–1873)
summary: Mill was a classical-liberal utilitarian who defended individual liberty limited only by harm to others, representative government with proportional representation, and equal rights for women. In political economy he favoured laisser-faire as a general rule with wide exceptions, taxation of unearned wealth, trade unions and peasant property, and in later life looked to worker co-operatives and open experiments in socialism while rejecting central planning. He also held that benevolent despotism could be legitimate over peoples he deemed barbarians.

ban-interest.rationale: Condemned usury laws, which cap interest, as a mischievous interference rooted in religious prejudice, endorsing Bentham's attack on them.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Described voting the taxes as the duty most peculiarly belonging to a representative assembly and approved the practice that supplies can only be voted by the House of Commons.

central-planning.rationale: Called the idea of conducting a country's whole industry by direction from a single centre obviously chimerical.

character-from-environment.rationale: Held character differences are explained largely by education and circumstances and called for study of the laws of the influence of circumstances on character.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Wrote that it is highly desirable subsistence be guaranteed by law to the destitute rather than depend on voluntary charity, which gives too much in one place and too little in another; private charity should handle discriminating between cases.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Wrote that despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians provided the end is their improvement, and that a free people may rule a less advanced one as a trust for its improvement.

class-collaboration.rationale: Expected the relation of masters and workpeople to be superseded by partnership and favoured industrial partnership and profit sharing; he also described labourers and employers as groups with divergent apparent interests.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Argued workers need concerted association to bargain over wages and that unions are the instrument that makes the labour market free.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Argued dependencies must be governed for the benefit of the governed, and that a country is not warranted in doing to other countries for its supposed benefit what it would not do to other people.

conscription.rationale: Listed bearing one's fair share in the common defence among positive acts that a person may rightfully be compelled to perform.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Said he was not charmed with an ideal of life as struggling to get on, trampling and elbowing, and that the best state for people is one where minds are not engrossed by the art of getting on.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Found a Fourierist community attractive and requiring less of common humanity than other socialist systems and wanted it tried, but treated the question as open and did not propose reorganising all society that way.

death-penalty.rationale: In April 1868 he spoke in the Commons against abolishing capital punishment, favouring retention for aggravated murder.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Supported a legal guarantee of subsistence for the destitute, including the able-bodied, over voluntary charity, while insisting relief be less eligible than independent labour to avoid pauperising dependency.

decide-locally.rationale: Argued in Considerations ch. XV that only a small portion of public business can be well done by central authorities and that local business should be handled by separate local representative bodies, with central authority supplying uniform principles.

democracy-best.rationale: Argued representative government is the ideally best form, favouring universal but graduated suffrage and proportional representation to guard against class legislation by a numerical majority.

direct-votes.rationale: Wrote that since citizens cannot all take part personally beyond a small town, the ideal government is representative, with the assembly controlling rather than doing the legislative work.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Wrote that the question of which government a people unites with ought to be decided by the governed.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Argued that fixing in advance by law that certain persons are unfit for certain occupations is wrong, and that legal subordination should be replaced by perfect equality.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Chaired the Jamaica Committee, which sought the prosecution of Governor Eyre for the martial-law killings, arguing the issue was whether dependencies would be governed by law or military licence.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Argued that eccentricity is desirable precisely because the tyranny of opinion makes it a reproach, and that the mere refusal to bend the knee to custom is itself a service.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Treated everybody's happiness as counting equally ('everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one') and opposed legal inequality between sexes.

experts-over-public.rationale: Favoured giving educated voters plural votes and having laws drafted by a small Commission of Legislation, while keeping the elected assembly in ultimate control.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Argued equal sacrifice means taxing incomes at the same percentage above an exempt minimum and that a graduated income tax penalises industry and saving, while favouring graduation for legacy duties.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Supported the Union's war against Confederate secession, but because it was undertaken to protect slavery, so the case is not a general rule.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Held that rival economic systems, including communist and co-operative communities, should get a fair trial, and defended experiments in living.

free-trade.rationale: Treated free trade as beneficial and the economic advantages of commerce as surpassed by its intellectual and moral effects; criticised protection as erroneous.

future-generations.rationale: Hoped for the sake of posterity that population and wealth would not grow until nature's beauty and wild places were extirpated.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Wrote that what is called the nature of women is an eminently artificial thing, the result of forced repression and unnatural stimulation, while holding natural differences cannot be known under present conditions.

harm-principle.rationale: His central doctrine: the only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over any member of a civilised community against his will is to prevent harm to others.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Wrote that the most vulgar way to escape consideration of social and moral influences is attributing diversities of conduct and character to inherent natural differences, using the Irish case.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Criticised a society where reward is in inverse ratio to labour and where birth decides rewards; looked to a time when the rule that they who do not work shall not eat applies to all and division follows an acknowledged principle of justice.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Called land the original inheritance of the whole species whose private appropriation is a question of expediency and ceases to be defensible where owners are not improvers; proposed state regulation or purchase in Ireland rather than general national ownership.

land-value-tax.rationale: Proposed special taxation of the unearned future rise in land rent, with owners compensated at current market value, but did not propose replacing most other taxes with it; contested fit.

legalize-drugs.rationale: In On Liberty called the Maine Law prohibition of liquor and the ban on opium imports into China violations of the buyer's liberty, while accepting labelling or licensing of dangerous poisons and taxes on intoxicants.

limit-growth.rationale: Hoped for posterity's sake that society would be content with a stationary state of capital and population, preserving solitude and natural beauty, with continued moral and social improvement.

limit-population.rationale: Wrote that conscientious restraint on population is indispensable, that laws forbidding marriage without means to support a family are within the state's legitimate powers, and recalled the Malthusian population principle as a banner of his youthful circle.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Argued that because gas and water companies are practical monopolies, such services should be performed by municipal authorities paid by a local rate, and listed hospitals among things government may need to provide where private effort fails.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Wrote that laisser-faire should be the general practice and every departure from it, unless required by some great good, is a certain evil; but he also listed large exceptions (monopolies, education, poor relief, public works).

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Mixed: allowed that some peoples will accept only certain ruling families and valued a limited monarch in some circumstances, while arguing representative government is the ideal and noting royalty as the one remaining office assigned by birth.

national-self-determination.rationale: Wrote that where the sentiment of nationality exists there is a prima facie case for uniting the nationality under its own government, though he also thought some small nationalities benefit from absorption.

natural-rulers.rationale: Mixed: favoured extra votes for educated citizens and representatives of higher intellect, but rejected rank, sex or race as grounds for exclusion from political rights.

office-by-exam.rationale: Advocated competitive examinations for admission to public employment, praising the Indian service model and urging that it be extended.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Wrote that the representative assembly must hold control of everything in the last resort, and that legislative control belongs to Parliament.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Rejected binding representatives to constituents' pledges and instructions, treating a representative as a trustee who must exercise judgement.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Called the legal subordination of one sex to the other wrong in itself and a chief hindrance to human improvement, and described the family as a school of despotism.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Held that restraint of population is indispensable to raise wages and that communism would not remove the need, yet he also blamed property laws and birth-determined distribution for poverty; mixed.

property-franchise.rationale: Mixed: opposed a property qualification and wanted universal suffrage, but would exclude people who cannot read, write and calculate, are on parish relief or do not pay taxes, and wanted taxation to reach the poorest class.

property-fundamental.rationale: Treated private property as justified by utility and subject to reform ('the principle of private property has never yet had a fair trial'); said landed property has no special sacredness and that the right of inheritance does not follow from it.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Held that property's justification is its general utility: when private property in land is not expedient it is unjust, and the laws of property have never conformed to the principle that justifies them.

proportional-representation.rationale: Strongly advocated Thomas Hare's system of personal representation as the greatest improvement of which representative government is susceptible.

public-ownership.rationale: Held that road, canal and railway monopolies should be reserved in reversion to the state or have their charges fixed by it, and that water and gas should be provided by municipal authorities paid by a local rate; allowed the state to own railways while companies operate them.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Cited a 21-month sentence in 1857 for offensive words about Christianity, and the rejection of jurors who professed no belief, as examples of persecution contrary to liberty of thought.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: In Principles Book II ch. XII he examined a legal minimum wage and argued that wages fixed above the market rate leave some workers jobless unless work or wages are guaranteed to all who apply; he preferred restraint of population and workers' own combination.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Said resisting oppression is a sacred right, and led the effort to prosecute a governor who, in his view, had put military licence in place of law.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Wrote that the principle of property cannot apply to the raw material of the earth, no one made the land, and it is a hardship to find nature's gifts engrossed; supported special taxation of land rent.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Said vituperative and offensive language should be discouraged by opinion, while law and authority have no business restraining it; allowed punishment only where words are direct incitement to mischief.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Condemned laws against combinations of workmen as the spirit of the slave-master and defended strikes as a legitimate collective action; did not take up picketing or strike ballots.

right-to-secede.rationale: Mixed: wrote that secession may be laudable or an enormous crime depending on its object, and condemned the Confederacy's separation to preserve slavery.

school-vouchers.rationale: Proposed that government require education for every child but leave parents to obtain it where and how they please, helping pay school fees of the poorer class, rather than providing schools itself.

second-chamber.rationale: Wrote in Considerations ch. XIII that he set little value on a second chamber's check on democracy and that, if other constitutional questions are rightly decided, it is of comparatively little importance whether there are two chambers or one.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Led the Jamaica Committee's effort to bring Governor Eyre and subordinates before criminal courts for the 1865 killings by courts-martial; a case of accountability of officials rather than of governments in general.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Insisted the utilitarian standard is not the agent's own happiness but the happiness of all concerned.

self-ownership.rationale: Wrote that over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.

separated-powers.rationale: Argued that a representative assembly should control government but not itself administer or draft laws, favouring separate executive departments and a legislative commission.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Argued marriage should be a partnership of equals like a business partnership, with no legal presumption of the husband's authority.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: In The Contest in America he identified slavery as the cause: the Southern leaders broke away on the ground that restraining the spread of slavery would be attempted.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Opened On Liberty with the history of limits placed on rulers' power, and favoured government under law rather than arbitrary rule.

state-harmful.rationale: Listed many necessary and optional functions of government and argued laisser-faire is only a general rule, not an abolition of the state.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Condemned protection as an interference grounded on erroneous theories; allowed protecting duties only temporarily, especially in a young nation, to naturalise an industry suited to the country.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Proposed fixing a maximum that any person may acquire by bequest or inheritance, and called graduated legacy and inheritance duties just and expedient even though he rejected graduation in general taxation.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Mixed: rejected a graduated income tax as a penalty on industry and saving, yet called graduated legacy and inheritance duties just, and wanted unearned fortunes and land-rent increases limited or specially taxed.

taxation-theft.rationale: Treated taxation as a legitimate state function and set out principles for equitable taxation.

unions-good.rationale: Wrote it is a great error to condemn trade unions or strikes per se and that associations of labourers are the necessary instrumentality of a free labour market; also cautioned about what strikes can achieve.

war-builds-character.rationale: Wrote that war in a good cause is not the greatest evil, that war is an ugly thing but not the ugliest, and that a decayed moral and patriotic feeling which thinks nothing worth a war is worse.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Praised peasant proprietorship as improving the condition and industry of the people, urged forming peasant properties on Irish waste lands in 1846-47, and proposed that Irish tenants have fixed tenure at assessed rents.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Criticised the law under which a wife's property and earnings pass absolutely to her husband, and sought equality in legal rights.

women-suffrage.rationale: Campaigned for women's suffrage, introduced the amendment to substitute 'person' for 'man' in the 1867 Reform Bill, and argued in The Subjection of Women and Considerations that sex is irrelevant to political rights.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Endorsed the principle of the 1834 Poor Law that relief should be less eligible than independent labour and noted public relief is refused to those who could get work and will not accept it.

worker-ownership.rationale: Wrote that the form of association expected to predominate as mankind improves is the labourers themselves, collectively owning the capital and working under managers they elect and can remove; the Autobiography calls co-operative societies socialistic experiments he welcomed.

notes: His views shifted toward socialism after 1848: later editions of the Principles and the posthumous Socialism chapters treat worker co-operatives and socialist experiments sympathetically, and these later positions are used where they differ from the first edition. Principles Book II-V text was read from econlib (full text), since the Gutenberg edition (#30107) is an abridgement that omits Book V ch. VII-XI. Positions marked 'Inferred' rest on his stated principles rather than direct statements.
